highlight.text: Munch chose heavily grained blocks of wood, allowing the pattern of the board to add texture to the scene, and he exploited the handmade aspect of the technique by carving blocks crudely. He also experimented so that each impression is unique, using black ink on the woodblock and watercolor and gouache to color the sheet extensively.

work.text: Two woodcuts were created in 1896 and 1902. In Gerd Woll's catalogue raisonné of all of Munch's prints, they are called Evening. Melancholy I and Melancholy III. … However, only the 1902 version retains the direction of the paintings, while the 1896 version is mirrored.

Like the lithograph, the woodcut gave rich possibilities for experiment … The woodcuts were mostly printed by Munch himself. Sometimes he sawed out a part of the plate to colour it differently from the rest.

source.author: J. P. Hodin
source.title: “Edvard Munch's Graphic Art”, in Edvard Munch: Etchings, Woodcuts and Lithographs (exhibition catalogue)

moment.text: It is an extremely moving picture, solemn and serious—almost religious. … He is the only one and the first to commit himself to idealism and dare to make nature, the model, etc., the vehicle for his mood and thus achieve more. Has anyone ever heard such a sound of color as in this painting?

moment.text: Influenced by Gauguin, as well as the etchings of German artist Max Klinger, Munch experimented with prints as a medium to create graphic versions of his works. In 1896 he created his first woodcuts—a medium that proved ideal to Munch's symbolic imagery.

matters.text: The boat gets smaller and smaller – the strokes of the oars echo across the surface of the sea – I was alone – the waves glided monotonously up to him – and lapped against the stone

matters.text: Evening, Melancholy I depicts the jilted, tormented art critic Jappe Nilssen, Munch's friend, on the shore of Åsgårdstrand, a fishing village south of Oslo.
The relationship awakened memories in Munch of his own, only a few years earlier and equally unhappy, love for Milly Thaulow.
